plain_title: When the body freezes, or won't stop moving
one_liner: Markedly reduced or unusual movement and responsiveness, from frozen stillness to agitation, occurring in many conditions.
in_simple_words: Catatonia is a syndrome of body and mind that can appear with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, severe depression, autism, or medical illness. A person may become almost completely still and silent, hold odd postures for hours, resist being moved, repeat others' words or movements, or, less often, become extremely agitated. It's often missed, and it's a medical priority: untreated, it can cause dehydration, clots, and a dangerous 'malignant' form. The good news is that it usually responds quickly to treatment.
what_it_can_feel_like: My daughter stopped speaking and sat staring for two days. We thought it was depression. It was catatonia, and one injection brought her back.
I could hear everything. I just couldn't make my body answer.
ECT sounded terrifying. It ended the catatonia in a week, and I'm grateful.
common_signs: Staying almost motionless, or holding unusual postures for long periods
Not speaking (mutism), or not responding to what's around them
Resisting instructions or being moved; or doing the opposite of what's asked
Not eating or drinking, which becomes dangerous

myths_vs_facts.fact: It's actually more common with mood disorders, and occurs in autism and medical illnesses too. It's now classified as a syndrome that can accompany many conditions.

myths_vs_facts.myth: A catatonic person isn't aware of anything.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Many people later describe being fully aware but unable to respond. Talking to them kindly matters.

myths_vs_facts.myth: There's nothing to do but wait.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Catatonia often responds within hours to days to benzodiazepines, and to ECT when those fail. Waiting is dangerous.

how_common.plain: Catatonia affects around 1 in 10 people admitted to hospital with serious mental illness, and is often unrecognized.
how_common.figure: Estimated at roughly 10% of acute psychiatric inpatients in some studies (DSM-5-TR text and reviews)

what_helps.plain_summary: Catatonia is treated urgently. Benzodiazepines (usually lorazepam), prescribed and monitored by a doctor, often bring rapid improvement, sometimes within hours. If they don't, electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is highly effective and can be life-saving. The underlying condition, whether a mood disorder, psychosis, or medical illness, is treated alongside. Supportive care, including fluids, nutrition, and preventing blood clots, is essential. Antipsychotics are used cautiously, as some can worsen catatonia.
evidence_based_options: Benzodiazepines, prescribed and monitored by a doctor, as first-line treatment
Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) when benzodiazepines don't work or the situation is dangerous
Treatment of the underlying mood, psychotic, or medical condition
Supportive medical care: hydration, nutrition, clot prevention
self_help_that_supports_care: For family: describing what you've seen to clinicians in detail, including how long it's lasted
Speaking to the person as if they can hear; they often can
Afterwards: helping the person make sense of what happened

when_to_reach_out: If someone has become unusually still, silent, or unresponsive, holds strange postures, or has stopped eating and drinking, get medical help today. This is an emergency if they have a fever, rigid muscles, or rapid changes in heart rate or blood pressure.
is_not: Severe depression can slow a person right down without catatonia; stupor from drugs, stroke, or other medical causes needs its own assessment. Autistic shutdown is different, though autistic people can develop catatonia.
hope_note: Catatonia is one of the most dramatically treatable conditions in psychiatry. People who were frozen for days are often talking and eating within a week.

in_young_people: Catatonia in children and teens is rare and often linked to autism, mood disorders, or medical conditions. It's frequently missed; a child who stops moving, speaking, or eating needs urgent assessment.

sub_sections.title: How it's coded
sub_sections.text: Catatonia associated with another mental disorder (a specifier), catatonic disorder due to another medical condition, and unspecified catatonia (coded with R29.818 first) all use F06.1.
